hints: Count the carbons carefully, the starting haloalkane has 3 carbons but the final acid has 4, so something must add a carbon in stage 1.
Remember which nucleophile adds exactly one extra carbon to a haloalkane to make a nitrile, $\text{R-I} \rightarrow \text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$.
Think about what happens to that nitrile in stage 2, since acid hydrolysis of a nitrile is the classic way to get a carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
**Spot the chain extension**

Look at the formulas side by side. You start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I}$ (3 carbons) and finish with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ (4 carbons).

So stage 1 cannot just swap I for another group, it must add one carbon.

**Recall the nitrile route**

The classic way to add one carbon to a halogenoalkane is nucleophilic substitution with cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$, heated in ethanol.

$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{I} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{CN} + \text{I}^-$$
The product is butanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$.

**Link to stage 2**

In stage 2, the nitrile is hydrolysed by heating with aqueous acid to give the carboxylic acid.

$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_4^+$$
That two-step sequence only works if stage 1 uses ethanolic potassium cyanide.

options.A: Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives nucleophilic substitution of I by OH to form propan-1-ol, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}$. No extra carbon is added, so you could never reach the 4-carbon acid.
options.B: Ethanolic ammonia gives nucleophilic substitution to form the amine, propylamine $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{NH}_2$. This keeps 3 carbons and does not lead to a carboxylic acid on hydrolysis.
options.C: Ethanolic potassium cyanide provides $\text{CN}^-$ which substitutes for I to give butanenitrile, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{CN}$. This adds the needed fourth carbon, and acid hydrolysis then gives butanoic acid.
options.D: Ethanolic sodium hydroxide causes elimination, not substitution, to give the alkene propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. This loses HI and does not extend the chain.
